title: Man Bites Dog(1992) I Don't Get it

commenti.body: I recall being blown away by that movie, it was completely wild and I loved the meta film crew filming aspect that shook the sense of reality. Then I met people who made it at a part, that was fantastic to chat about it.

There's not much to "get". It's black humor and you seem to be offended by black humor.

One important aspect is that it spoofs an early 90's Belgian phenomenon: TV show "Striptease". It also references the murder of Grégory Villemin. It's more enjoyable when you know what it references.

>the movie asks us to take Ben's opinion on low income housing seriously

No it doesn't, why do you think it does? The guy is literally a psychopath. It's the gap between his actions and his musings about architecture which is funny. But if I have to explain how it's funny, means you're not receptive to this kind of humor.

>The camera cuts to the aftermath of the attack where her body is mutilated and her husbands neck is cut.

You must have seen the censored version.

One way to approach it might be from a satirical perspective exploring how movies, and audiences, engage with violence: lasciviously, pruriently, pretentiously, luridly, exploitatively, moralistically and morally dubiously, comedically, and ultimately, with a potential degree of culpability. 

It's not subtle by any means, but back on release it nailed something in the zeitgeist. We'd come out of the formalist video nasty era and were entering the post-modern violence of the Tarrantino era. Violence in movies was a very hot topic.Today, it perhaps has more relevance to the True Crime docs popularised by Netflix. 

However, if you didn't find it funny, then it's unlikely you ever will. And that's fine too. We're not supposed to like everything.

I think the humor comes from the juxtaposition of the serious subject matter and the tropes of a mockumentary. The camera crew after the murder is humorous because you jump from the seriousness of the murder to the mundane nature of the camera crew recording it. 

It’s humorous that the crew is more concerned with the documentary than the murders. 

I don’t remember the scene exactly, but I think the heart medication is also humorous due to his blasé attitude. It’s as if he is demonstrating the best way to perform a simple task and he is happy that there is an even simpler way.

I disagree that the movie asks us to take Ben’s opinion on low income housing seriously. I saw it again as a documentary trope (asking the subject about politics) applied to serial killing.

I loved the first half of the movie and then I got bored when I realized it was the same joke over and over.

This is spot on, IMO. I saw Man Bites Dog at the time of release and it did indeed feel like much sharper satire than I guess it would now (though I haven't seen it in a good few years).   


I'd add that it didn't just seem to be purely about representations of violence. It also commented on, and pre-figured the absolute explosion in, so-called "reality" TV, where the very same collusion of viewer and filmmakers in terms of exploitation practically became the "point" of certain TV shows. In this respect, MBD was less about violence and more about encouraging or endorsing unethical behaviour in the name of supposedly documenting something real (notwithstanding the irony of these situations usually being entirely set up and unlikely to have even occurred in the absence of  camera crew/presenter/audience and all the other machinery of TV).

Concur completely.
It absolutely pre-empted the Reality TV M.O.: locate individuals with borderline personality issues and place them under observation until transgressive behaviour occurs. If said behaviour is unforthcoming, construct provocative situations to assist in its emergence. Call it a "social experiment" and absolve oneself of all responsibility. All the while the audience eggs everyone along from the comfort of the sofa. This was 00s TV in a nutshell.

It's a media satire. It is about how the "journalists" lose their distance and become part of the story and become complicit in the crimes, just like when journalists give  attention to extremists and then pretend to be shocked by the awful behavior of the extremists and the popularity they get from attention, or when they give attention to people who self-harm and feign shock that the behavior is contagious.

>I loved the first half of the movie and then I got bored when I realized it was the same joke over and over.

I don't think that's accurate, it gradually turns up the violence and grossness, until it makes the audience uneasy, or at least that's the intention. Even when they kill the middleclass family it's kinda funny, but then there's a *very* graphic rape/murder-scene, and when that happened, the mood changed a lot in the cinema where I saw it. You're supposed to feel like an accomplice by the end.

Also concur. That's another aspect. You could perhaps even call that the ur-text.
I did say "One way" to approach it in my original response...
You can't say that and not elaborate, any interesting details you can remember?

it didnt fully click for me either, some of it was hilarious cuz of how bizarre it is and other parts are just ok or tiring. The camera crew slowly becoming part of his crimes and not caring about the murders is funny. and i thought killing the woman by scaring her is funny.

I think in the context of it being a student film and this insane french dude its funny (not always laugh out loud funny but like smiling to myself funny)

Well,for one I loved the movie and they said it was surprising how few people seemed to appreciate it so much. Well, in a way what do you expect? ;) They were great people, very friendly, down to earth, they seemed extremely happy to be discussing the work they put so much time and effort into. I told them how that whole scene with the kid going back, as kids will, was fun and disturbing. I recall we chatted about the meta aspect of the doc forcing viewers into a position of questioning what was real. I was younger then and I didn't know who they were then. Today I'd have much more to talk about.

I loved Man Bites Dog and found it wickedly funny. But I love black comedy (Delicatessen, Brazil, and Fargo are some other favorites of mine, off the top of my head). But then I laughed out loud many times watching American Psycho in a movie theater in Dallas. No one else laughed, so who knows what they thought about me 😂

When I watched this movie, it left me thinking about how most movies aren’t that different from this one. We’re watching this serial killer have a good time, crack jokes, and murder people. What’s a marvel movie? It’s really just watching mass murders have a good time, team up, and kill people. Yeah, they’re not “bad guys”, but why aren’t they? In fact, so much of the media we consume we cheer for the “good guys” who aren’t really that much different from the killer in this movie.


You watch spider man joke around and pummel some people, and ultimately that’s not really different from watching Ben. So why is marvel good fun wholesome entertainment for the family, and Man bites dog grotesque? It says a lot about us.
